Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

occupy verb

take and hold a place

also occupation (of a country), take over, seize, hold (a place), occupied (territory), the seat is taken

classical

Cic. Agr. 2.75: tōtam Ītaliam suīs praesidiīs obsidēre atque occupāre (Lewis & Short)
Hor. C. 1.14.2: occupā portum

occupō, occupāre, occupāvī, occupātum

verb, first conjugation

seize, take possession of, occupy

To seize, often before someone else can: a hill, a harbour, a seat. Its other senses: to fill or take up (time, space), to keep someone busy (see occupy-busy), to fall on someone, and to be first to do something: occupet extrēmum scabiēs, last one there’s a rotten egg (Hor. A.P. 417).

Other words

  • teneō, tenēre, tenuī, tentum — hold (a place)

    verb, second conjugation · also used · classical · Caes. B.C. 1.44: legiō locum nōn tenuit (Lewis & Short); Caes. B.G. 3.2: montēs tenērī

    Of keeping a place once taken: a position, a seat.

  • obsideō, obsidēre, obsēdī, obsessum — besiege; hold with troops

    verb, second conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Agr. 2.75 (Lewis & Short)

    Properly to sit before a town, besiege or blockade it; then to beset and hold a place.

Examples

  • occupat hic collem, cumbā sedet alter aduncā et dūcit rēmōs illīc, ubi nūper arābat

    one takes to a hill, another sits in a curved boat and rows where lately he was ploughingOv. Met. 1.293–294

  • dictū mīrābile, tenuit nōn sōlum āles captam semel sēdem

    wonderful to tell, the bird not only kept the seat it had once takenLiv. 7.26.5

See also occupy, capture, free, war.
